paras: The roping and banishment of a Hayesville man at Loudonville, Ohio, took place on Saturday, March 26, 1881, when a group of townspeople took an unnamed man from the town marshal, put a rope around his neck and drove him from town. He was released after swearing never to return, and no paper stated his race. A Cleveland dispatch about the affair ran in papers across the country under approving headlines such as "Served Him Right."

According to the Cleveland dispatch, a "bully" from Haysville, Ohio, came to Loudonville on the Saturday and, "among other reprehensible acts," insulted the editors of the two papers published there. The Chicago Daily Tribune called him a "thug" from the neighboring village of Hayesville and said he insulted several residents before trying to intimidate two editors.

The town marshal arrested the man, but half a dozen citizens took him away from the officer. In the wire version they gave him a "liberal castigation," put a rope around his neck, led him beyond the town line and made him swear never to show his face in Loudonville again. The Chicago account said nothing of a beating: the citizens assembled, roped him, led him around the town and then let him leave on his promise not to return.
No report of any arrest or charge against the citizens appears in the coverage, and the man's name was never printed.

The story reached readers mainly as a short Cleveland dispatch dated March 28, which the Washington Evening Star printed that day under the head "Served Him Right." Over the following days it appeared in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "Learned a Lesson," in the Eureka Daily Sentinel as "Never to Show His Face" and in the New-York Tribune as "An Ohio Bully Summarily Dealt With." Western weeklies such as the Helena Weekly Herald and the Bismarck Tribune were still running it in crime roundups at the start of April.

The headlines took the townspeople's side, and the Chicago Daily Tribune opened its own paragraph by remarking that Loudonville had "a way of their own for dealing with roughs." None of the reports mentioned race, and no account from the man himself or from a local Ohio paper was found.

The versions differ on whether he was beaten, with the wire reporting a "castigation" and the Chicago paragraph omitting it. They also differ on whether he was led beyond the town line or around Loudonville, though both end with his leaving on a pledge to stay away.

bases: Half a dozen citizens took a man from the town marshal, administered a 'castigation', put a rope around his neck and drove him from town, with no killing (A1, A16, A17); A4 reports the roping and banishment without the beating.

Every copy is the same Cleveland, March 28 wire item (A1, A16, A17 and the reprints); the Chicago Daily Tribune paragraph (A4) is worded differently but reports nothing that shows a separate source, and no local Ohio report was found.

record_check.dossier: No paper states the man's race; nothing in the coverage identifies him as Black, so the episode's place among anti-Black violence is unsupported.
No pursuit; arrest by the marshal, seizure from the marshal, a 'castigation' (wire only), rope around the neck, led out of town, oath to stay away.
The papers say 'liberal castigation', 'severe castigation' or 'liberal chastisement', not whipping; the Chicago version mentions no beating.
No county is named in the coverage; the papers give only Loudonville, Ohio.

Unnamed 'citizens' of Loudonville, half a dozen by the wire count.
